title: How to enlarge cursor in PowerPoint on Mac for better visibility and easier navigation
metaTitle: How to enlarge cursor on Mac for PowerPoint
description: Learn how to enlarge cursor on Mac to improve visibility in PowerPoint. Follow these system-wide steps to adjust your pointer size for better accessibility.
targetKeyword: how to enlarge cursor on mac
intro: You cannot change the cursor size inside the PowerPoint app itself, so you must adjust your Mac system settings. These changes apply globally to your entire computer, ensuring your cursor is easier to see while working in PowerPoint.
tldr: Open System Settings on your Mac.
Navigate to Accessibility and then Display.
Adjust the Pointer size slider to your preference.
Enable Shake to Locate for even better visibility.

blocks.text: Why you cannot change the cursor inside PowerPoint

Many users look for a setting inside PowerPoint to make their mouse pointer larger. Microsoft does not include this feature in the Mac version of PowerPoint. The application relies on the operating system to define how the cursor appears on your screen. This is standard behavior for most desktop applications on macOS. When you change your system settings, it affects how the cursor looks in PowerPoint, Excel, Word, and every other app you use. This ensures a consistent experience across your entire workspace.
How to enlarge cursor on Mac using System Settings
Adjusting the pointer size is a straightforward process in modern versions of macOS. Follow these steps to find the setting and customize your experience.

items: Click the Apple menu in the top-left corner of your screen.
Select System Settings from the dropdown menu.
Click on Accessibility in the left-hand sidebar.
Select Display from the list of options.
Find the Pointer section on the right side.
Drag the Pointer size slider to the right to make it larger.

blocks.text: You will notice the change immediately. Move your mouse around your slide deck to see if the new size works for you. If it is still too small, you can drag the slider further. If it feels too clunky, slide it back to the left. You can also change the Pointer outline color and Pointer fill color in this same window. Many users find that a high-contrast outline, such as black or bright blue, makes the cursor much easier to track against white slide backgrounds.

If you do not want a permanently large cursor, consider the Shake to Locate feature. This is one of the most effective ways to find your mouse on a busy slide. When enabled, you can quickly wiggle your finger on the trackpad or flick your mouse. The cursor will temporarily grow to a very large size, making it impossible to lose. This is particularly helpful if you are presenting on a large external monitor or using multiple screens.

items: Go to System Settings > Accessibility > Display.
Toggle the switch for Shake mouse pointer to locate to the On position.

blocks.text: Sometimes the problem is not the mouse pointer, but the thin blinking line when you are typing text. This insertion point can be hard to see in a large text box. macOS offers a specific tool for this as well. Go to System Settings > Accessibility > Text Cursor. Here you can enable the Text Cursor Indicator. This adds a colored highlight around your text cursor. You can choose a color that stands out against your slide themes. This makes it much easier to see exactly where your next character will appear.

Some users report that they cannot find the slider. This usually happens if you are looking in the Mouse or Trackpad menus. Those menus control speed and gesture sensitivity, not the visual size of the pointer. Always ensure you are in the Accessibility menu. If you are using an older version of macOS, the menu might be called System Preferences instead of System Settings. The steps remain the same, but the labels might differ slightly. If you feel the cursor is still not visible enough, consider checking your display resolution settings. Sometimes a very high resolution makes all interface elements appear smaller than intended.

Digital accessibility is not just about meeting requirements. It is about reducing the strain of your daily work. When you spend hours building presentations, small adjustments to your interface can prevent eye fatigue. Using a larger cursor or the text cursor indicator helps you maintain focus on your content. It allows you to move faster and make fewer mistakes during the design process. These small changes lead to a more comfortable and efficient way of working on your Mac.

faq.question: Does changing the cursor size affect other apps?
faq.answer: Yes, changing the pointer size in System Settings is a global change. It will affect the cursor size in PowerPoint, Word, Chrome, and every other application on your Mac.

faq.question: Can I have a different cursor size just for PowerPoint?
faq.answer: No, macOS does not support application-specific cursor sizes. The settings you choose in Accessibility apply to the entire operating system.

faq.question: What is the Text Cursor Indicator?
faq.answer: It is an accessibility feature that adds a colored highlight around your blinking text insertion line. It makes it much easier to see where you are typing in a document or slide.

steps.name: Open System Settings
steps.text: Click the Apple menu () in the top-left corner of your screen, then select System Settings.

steps.name: Access Accessibility
steps.text: In the left sidebar, scroll down and click on Accessibility.

steps.name: Open Display Settings
steps.text: Click on the Display menu to see your visual options.

steps.name: Adjust Pointer Size
steps.text: Find the Pointer section and move the Pointer size slider to your desired level.

troubleshooting.fix: Ensure you are in the Accessibility menu, not the Mouse or Trackpad menu.

troubleshooting.problem: The text cursor is still hard to see.
troubleshooting.fix: Enable the Text Cursor Indicator in Accessibility > Text Cursor.
